title: ToF-PAX-RIXS: A Time-of-Flight Spectrometer for combined ARPES and RIXS
authors: Chafic Fawaz, Tom Lacmannn, Yaryna Lytvynenko, Sergii Chernov, Olena Tkach, Siegmar Roth, Jan O. Schunck, Amon Lanz, Jakob Dilling, Lukas Bruckmeier, Markus Scholz, Frank Scholz, Arne Meyer, Dirk Fuchs, Lara Schmieder, Yiran Liu, Matteo Minola, Bernhard Keimer, Dmytro Kutnyakhov, Kai Rossnagel, Olena Fedchenko, Angela Wittmann, Moritz Hoesch, Gerd Schönhense, Matthieu Le Tacon, Hans-Joachim Elmers, Martin Beye
abstract: We present ToF-PAX-RIXS, a compact instrument that combines time-of-flight momentum-microscopy angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) with resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS). The latter is based on photoelectron spectrometry for analysis of X-rays (PAX). The two techniques are implemented with a single multimode electron-optical column, allowing measurements to be performed sequentially on the same sample under identical experimental conditions. In ARPES mode, the instrument records the photoemission intensity as a function of kinetic energy and two in-plane momentum components. In PAX-RIXS mode, scattered soft X-ray photons are absorbed in a thin metallic converter, and the generated photoelectrons are analyzed in energy and position of emission on the converter. The electron kinetic energy retains the spectral information of the scattered photons, while the position is related to the scattering angle and therefore to the momentum transfer, enabling simultaneous access to a finite momentum-transfer interval. We describe the mechanical design, converter assembly, scattering geometry, and multimode electron optics of the instrument. Its PAX-RIXS performance is benchmarked at the Cu $L_3$ edge using CaCuO$_2$, with Au, Ag, and Pt converters. The measured spectra reproduce the principal features obtained with a conventional grating RIXS spectrometer, and deconvolution yields an effective reconstructed energy resolution better than $120$~meV under the present conditions. Finally, combined ARPES and PAX-RIXS measurements on the same Ca-doped YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.45}$ sample demonstrate the capability of the instrument to correlate electronic structure and collective excitations within a common compact platform.
summary: This paper introduces ToF-PAX-RIXS, a novel, compact instrument that merges Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES) with Resonant Inelastic X-ray Scattering (RIXS). By using Photoelectron Spectrometry (PAX) for RIXS analysis, the instrument can measure both single-particle electronic structure and collective excitations on the same sample. This capability is crucial for understanding the complex physics of strongly correlated materials like high-Tc superconductors.
main_problem: The need for complementary experimental probes to achieve a comprehensive microscopic description of quantum materials, which exhibit complex electronic behavior arising from interactions between electrons and collective excitations.
main_result: The development and demonstration of ToF-PAX-RIXS, a compact instrument capable of correlating single-particle electronic structure (ARPES) and collective excitations (RIXS) on the same sample platform.
method: The instrument combines Time-of-Flight ARPES with RIXS analyzed via Photoelectron Spectrometry (PAX), allowing sequential measurements on the same sample under identical conditions.
model_or_system: The platform is designed for studying quantum materials, specifically demonstrated on Ca-doped YBa2Cu3O6.45, which are strongly correlated cuprate superconductors. The technique measures photoemission intensity and scattered X-ray photon spectral information.
key_observables: Photoemission intensity $I(E_{kin}, k_x, k_y)$ (ARPES) and electron energy/position from photoelectrons generated by absorbed soft X-rays (RIXS).
important_parameters: Energy resolution better than 120 meV; momentum transfer ($\mathbf{Q}$) accessible via photoelectron position.
main_assumptions: The measurement relies on the ability to analyze photoelectrons generated from absorbed soft X-rays (PAX) to reconstruct the RIXS spectrum, circumventing the need for large, conventional RIXS spectrometers.
figures_summary: Figures detail the mechanical design, CAD overview, and schematic configurations for both ARPES and RIXS measurement modes on the instrument.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the scientific need for combined ARPES and RIXS measurements, details the technical solution using the ToF-PAX-RIXS instrument, benchmarks its performance using $	ext{CaCuO}_2$, and finally demonstrates the combined capability on a cuprate superconductor.
why_interesting: The ability to combine two powerful, yet technically disparate, spectroscopic techniques (ARPES and RIXS) into one compact platform is highly valuable for condensed matter theorists studying correlated electron systems, as it provides simultaneous access to single-particle and collective excitation spectra.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Sketch of the dual-use detector system. (a) PAX-RIXS mode, where the electron optics are set to PEEM mode, imaging the converter surface in a large field of view of several mm in diameter. The sample and converter are shown on a larger scale. (b) Momentum microscopy mode, where the converter has been removed and the electron optics image direct photoelectrons after refocusing the objective lens.
Figure 2: (Left) CAD overview of the assembled ToF-PAX-RIXS spectrometer. (Right) The set-up installed on beamline P04 at DESY.
Figure 3: (Left) CAD overview and (middle) the realized setup of the sample chamber. (Right) Translation and rotation degrees of freedom of the sample and converters.

Figure 4: ToF-PAX-RIXS measurement configurations. (a) ARPES configuration, where the red cone represents the photo-emitted electrons. (b) RIXS configuration, where the blue cone represents the inelastic photons, and the red rectangle represents the photo-emitted electrons converted from these inelastic photons, allowing us to measure the PAX-RIXS spectrum.

Figure 5: Converter assembly. (a) Schematic of the Au converter, consisting of a thin aluminum foil coated with an ultrathin gold layer as the conversion material. (b) Converter assembly holding different converters and an alignment grid.
